title: Socrates and the Oracle of Delphi: 'The Wisest Man Knows He Knows Nothing'
summary: When the Oracle of Delphi proclaimed Socrates the wisest man in Greece, Socrates set out to test the riddle, concluding that true wisdom lies in recognizing one's own ignorance.
full_text:
In fifth-century BCE Greece, Chaerephon, an impetuous companion of Socrates, journeyed to the sacred sanctuary of the sun archer at Delphi and asked the Pythian priestess:
"Is there any man living wiser than Socrates?"
The Oracle delivered an unequivocal response: "No man is wiser than Socrates."

When Chaerephon returned to Athens and reported the divine prophecy, Socrates was deeply bewildered:
"Whatever can the god mean? For I am conscious in myself that I possess no profound wisdom whatsoever. The god cannot tell an untruth; yet how can I be the wisest of men?"

To solve the divine riddle, Socrates embarked upon a famous quest. He sought out those with the highest reputations for knowledge—prominent politicians, celebrated epic poets, and master craftsmen—and engaged them in rigorous examination.

Socrates uncovered a startling paradox:
The politicians spoke with supreme eloquence, yet when pressed for principles of justice, they had none. The poets composed verses by divine inspiration, yet could not explain their meaning. The craftsmen mastered their technical arts, yet mistakenly assumed they were equally expert in the highest matters of statecraft and virtue!

Walking home, Socrates reflected upon the Oracle's meaning:
"I am indeed wiser than this man. Neither of us knows anything really worth knowing; but he fancies he knows something when he knows nothing, whereas I, knowing nothing, do not fancy I know anything! In this one small degree, then, I am wiser: I do not deceive myself that I know what I do not know!"

The Delphic paradox established Socratic humility as the cornerstone of Western philosophy: the beginning of true wisdom is the candid recognition of one’s own ignorance.
